title: Poker Face
intro: A straight face holds together two different claims: I have principles, and nobody gets to tell me how to make art. Jackzebra moves from earning honestly and keeping his dignity to deliberately shameless jokes and his own rules. YoungQueenz then complicates the victory lap: the inventory of clothes, travel and desire also includes pain and unwanted enemies. The final line makes the face collective. Keeping this identity going can feel more natural than giving it up, even when it is no longer an uncomplicated success story.
reading: Dignity versus artistic shamelessness; guest verse interrupts a simple inventory of success.

revisions.poker-face-dignity: The claim about dignity follows two very practical assurances: he does not scam people, and he earns only a little. His face is therefore more than a fashionable expression of indifference. It stands for being able to answer for how he lives, despite lacking much money. That makes the later declaration of shamelessness interesting: he wants ethical credibility without accepting respectable limits on what an artist may say.
revisions.editorial-6-director: Calling himself the director gives him control over the scene he is making. The next image throws men and women into one cooking pot; the following joke turns being cooked into being familiar with people. The absurdity is the point: this is a world whose relations he can rearrange. When he subsequently calls these his rules and his content, the film metaphor becomes a claim to authorship, rather than simply another way to say he is important.
revisions.poker-face-dead-pig: A dead pig cannot be frightened with boiling water: the proverb describes someone beyond shame or intimidation. It cuts across his earlier insistence that people need dignity. The two statements can coexist if the distinction is between how he treats people and what he permits himself in art. He is asking to be respected while refusing to make respectability the test of his work. The lyric leaves that friction audible instead of neatly resolving it.
revisions.editorial-6-pain-inventory: YoungQueenz uses the same 'I got' construction for desirable possessions and for pain and enemies. The grammar makes the unwanted things arrive as part of the same package. Listen for the change from everything he wanted, to everything the listener wanted, to things he does not want at all. This guest verse gives the poker face something to conceal; the world-travelling success story comes with an emotional bill.
revisions.phrase-6-persistence: Persistence being easier than quitting reverses the familiar motivational slogan. Continuing may be less a heroic decision than the only way these performers know how to remain themselves. The last phrase says 'our face', turning the title from an individual pose into something shared. Coming after the guest's mixed inventory of success and pain, it sounds like commitment to an identity whose costs are already understood.
